extracted.intended_audience: public relations counselors / public relations students / practitioners
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for public-relations counsels on analyzing publics, selecting appeals, and designing methods to modify public opinion. Covers group analysis, instincts, stereotypes, changed conditions, media choice, and practical devices (committees, contests, publicity events).

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognize interlapping (overlapping) groups
rubrics_metrics.description: The public relations counsel must take into account that many groups exist, and that there is a very definite interlapping of groups.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Society consists of many overlapping groups (e.g., workers who are also capitalists, farmers who are tenants or owners). This interlapping enables use of many types of appeal to reach a single individual by the different groups to which he belongs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Subdivide audience into component groups
rubrics_metrics.description: Analyze and divide the public into component groups for the campaign's purposes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Federation for the Support of Jewish Charities subdivided into dentists, bankers, real-estate operators, motion-picture owners, etc., to approach each group on its strongest appeal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appeal to each group's strongest common interest
rubrics_metrics.description: Approach each group on the strongest appeal to which the members of the group as a group would respond.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Capitalize social aspirations, ambitions for leadership, competitive desires, philanthropic tendencies, or profession-specific interests when addressing that group.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use multiple appeals addressing an individual's multiple group identities
rubrics_metrics.description: Reach individuals by appeals that address the multiple group identities they possess (e.g., as humanitarian, public-spirited citizen, member of a religious group).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: By appealing to different identities, an organization can move the same person for the same cause via several different emotional or social routes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Analyze and adapt to changed external conditions
rubrics_metrics.description: Changed external conditions must be taken into account by the public relations counsel in his work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Changes (new media, technology, economic conditions, strikes, laws) modify interests and viewpoints. Example: radio increases contact with world events for farmers; automobile altered daily life and geography. Counsel must estimate differences produced and adapt strategy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interpret and emphasize changed conditions to modify public opinion
rubrics_metrics.description: The counsel can modify point of view by calling attention to or interpreting changed conditions in terms of the interest of those affected.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: for radio, counsel may enlarge radio's field or stress its importance to increase acceptance; for thrift campaigns, inflation made thrift messages more persuasive.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exploit universal instincts and basic desires
rubrics_metrics.description: Use fundamental human instincts (self-preservation, sex hunger, food hunger) in messaging.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Advertising examples: cozy home radiators appeal to shelter/self-preservation; food images appeal to gustatory sense; soap ads exploit sex/attraction. Tailor messages to these universal drives.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use McDougall's primary instincts as emotional levers
rubrics_metrics.description: Employ William McDougall's seven primary instincts and attendant emotions: flight-fear, repulsion-disgust, curiosity-wonder, pugnacity-anger, self-display-elation, self-abasement-subjection, parental-love-tenderness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Different instincts are used in different contexts: fear in public-health campaigns; curiosity via teasers and 'feelers'; pugnacity to create issues or contests; self-display to reward supporters; parental-love in charity appeals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use fear (flight) in public-health and safety messaging
rubrics_metrics.description: Stress possibility of danger or epidemic to appeal to fear and motivate preventive action.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Public-health campaigns use war-like language ('kill the germs', 'swat the fly') and quantify progress (annual victim counts) to sustain a combat frame that mobilizes public action.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use curiosity/wonder (suspense) to build interest
rubrics_metrics.description: Arouse curiosity in advance of announcements using feelers and teasers to increase public attention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Publishers and statesmen use suspense; examples include 'What is wrong with this picture?' ads or pre-announcement feelers to stimulate attention.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use pugnacity and contests to attract crowds and engagement
rubrics_metrics.description: Frame events as contests or issues to enlist pugnacity and draw larger, more engaged audiences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Debates and contests bring larger attendance than neutral lectures; allow 'talking back' to increase engagement. Use spectacle, resolution of protest, or identifiable antagonists to stimulate interest.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognize ethical/dangerous side of pugnacity
rubrics_metrics.description: Pugnacity can be enlisted for progress or can be used to suppress and oppress; dangers must be recognized.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Public relations counsel should weigh the ordinary dangers of a potent psychological weapon and avoid tactics that denigrate or unjustly manipulate audiences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use self-display/elation to deepen supporter commitment
rubrics_metrics.description: Publicly praise or honor supporters to increase their allegiance and activity on behalf of a cause.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: naming rooms/beds after donors, elaborate letterheads, public recognition which turns lukewarm adherents into forceful advocates.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use parental love/tenderness in appeals
rubrics_metrics.description: Employ imagery of children and parental tenderness to evoke strong philanthropic responses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Baby-kissing politicians or charity photos of starving children illustrate the effective use of parental-love appeals in fundraising and sympathy campaigns.

rubrics_metrics.name: Leverage gregariousness via group leaders
rubrics_metrics.description: Identify and enlist group leaders whose authority causes followers to join new causes they endorse.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Group leaders can carry multiple groups; securing a prominent individual's adherence may bring allied groups into alignment (example: a Republican leader endorsing the League of Nations).

rubrics_metrics.name: Select leaders strategically to represent varied stereotypes
rubrics_metrics.description: Choose leaders who collectively mirror the cross-section and stereotypes of the target public to reinforce credibility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Form committees including bankers, society women, lawyers, preachers, merchants to create a cross-sectional committee that concretizes the desired public impression (hotel anniversary example).

rubrics_metrics.name: Exploit individualism alongside group appeals
rubrics_metrics.description: Appeal to individuals' desire for self-expression as a complement to gregarious appeals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Combine self-display and individual recognition with group-based messages to meet both social and personal motives.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use acquisition and construction instincts where relevant
rubrics_metrics.description: Employ appeals to owning and building (e.g., 'Own your own home', 'Build your own home') when these instincts fit the campaign's objective.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These are minor instincts but useful for specific homeownership or construction-oriented campaigns.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exploit susceptibility to suggestion, imitation, habit, and play
rubrics_metrics.description: Use human tendencies toward imitation, habit, and play to design accessible, repeatable, and enjoyable events or messages.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: street fairs, fireworks, marble contests, horseshoe pitching — playful events mobilize participation and goodwill.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use stereotypes and mental habits as shortcuts
rubrics_metrics.description: Leverage existing mental stereotypes (stereotype of 'farmer', 'general', etc.) to transfer new ideas onto familiar images.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Counsel may use current stereotypes, combat them, or create new ones to carry desired associations; be mindful that overused stereotypes lose power.

rubrics_metrics.name: Create or combat stereotypes strategically
rubrics_metrics.description: Either reinforce friendly stereotypes (e.g., Danube waltz for Austria) or question hostile ones (put 'American' in quotes to remove patriotic association) to alter public perception.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use stereotype-shaping deliberately: bring forward favorable images, or diminish unwanted connotations to redirect sentiment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use visible objects and emblems as effective stereotypes
rubrics_metrics.description: Place visible props (national flag, instruments, white factory walls) to convey immediate stereotyping cues to audiences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Scientists should be shown with instruments; doctors with kits; food factories painted white to suggest cleanliness. Emblems and trademarks serve as visual shortcuts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Beware overuse of stereotypes
rubrics_metrics.description: Recognize that stereotypes can become 'shop-worn' and lose persuasive power through overuse.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Monitor audience fatigue (e.g., 'Hundred per cent American' died from overuse) and refresh messaging or create new imagery when necessary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use habit and stereotype to achieve gradual change (rearrangement)
rubrics_metrics.description: Progress often occurs by rearranging individuals' thoughts within overlapping groups rather than abrupt expulsion of old ideas.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Modify opinions stealthily via repeated, varied appeals that exploit habit and stereotype; gradual, directed change is often more successful.

rubrics_metrics.name: Follow a structured campaign process
rubrics_metrics.description: Analyze the client's problem and objective; analyze the public to be reached; devise a plan of action; determine methods and organs of distribution; estimate client-public interaction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This stepwise approach ensures coherent strategy: e.g., for a tariff bill, visualize many public perspectives (manufacturer, worker, politician) to craft appeals that hit multiple relevant groups.

rubrics_metrics.name: Visualize multiple public perspectives when designing appeals
rubrics_metrics.description: See the problem simultaneously from the vantage of many publics (manufacturer, retailer, importer, worker, financier, politician) to identify points of appeal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Within groups, consider subdivisions (e.g., manufacturers dependent on domestic vs. imported raw materials) to avoid misdirected appeals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choose channels/organs of distribution appropriate to subgroups
rubrics_metrics.description: Determine which media or institutions (schools, museums, newspapers, radio) will best reach each subgroup and tailor the message accordingly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: present silk as fashion to women's clubs, as art to museum-goers, as a natural-history lesson to schools, and as news to newspapers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use committees and contests to reinforce image and mobilize participation
rubrics_metrics.description: Organize anniversary committees, contests judged by recognized authorities, or prize events to attach stereotypes and mobilize engagement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hotel anniversary committee including prominent citizens bolsters prestige; a 'Bring home the Beech-Nut' sales contest with national sales managers as judges creates mass participation and brand association.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use 'feelers' and advance publicity to prime audiences
rubrics_metrics.description: Send out preliminary feelers to arouse public interest prior to full announcements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Governmental and publishing examples show that pre-release curiosity increases attention and attendance at the main event or announcement.
